findings.headline: Money market funds account for £10,120,000, 52% of the portfolio, the largest rating-exposure share in the report.

findings.matters: A large share held in money market funds, rather than fixed-term deposits, changes how quickly cash can be accessed and how exposure to a single fund manager is spread, which other councils will compare against their own treasury policies.

findings.headline: West Lindsey's total investments stand at £20,320,000 at a weighted rate of 4.06%, or 4.10% excluding its £1,000,000 property fund holding.

findings.matters: Slow follow-through on audit recommendations suggests weak governance culture and difficulty translating audit findings into operational change. This affects how quickly and effectively the council responds to control weaknesses.

findings.matters: A lender would need to understand this concentrated revenue dependency on a volatile asset class and assess the risk to the council if property values or rental income fall.
findings.figures: Commercial Income: £1.718m (2026/27); Net Revenue Expenditure: £21.414m; Ratio: 8%

findings.headline: Commercial property investment programme halted; no new acquisitions anticipated despite £30m budget approval
findings.detail: The council invested £21.666m in commercial property against an approved £30m budget. The strategy explicitly halts expansion: no new acquisitions are anticipated. The portfolio comprises 6 acquired properties (£20.5m excluding costs) and 6 recategorized assets, generating gross returns of 7.89% for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Commercial property was being deployed to generate revenue and support financial resilience. The halt to expansion indicates either market constraints or resource limitations affecting the council's income-generating strategy.
findings.figures: Commercial property investment: £21.666m deployed of £30m approved; Gross return 2025/26: 7.89%
findings.quote: It is no longer anticipated that additional assets will be acquired.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure projected to fall from £17.4m (2024/25) to £3.6m (2026/27), with 'Our Place' spending dropping 95%
findings.detail: Capital expenditure is projected to fall dramatically from £17.398m (2024/25) to £3.558m (2026/27) and further to £1.957m (2028/29). The 'Our Place' cluster drops from £10.592m to £0.476m in 2026/27, suggesting major infrastructure or place-making activities are being paused or reduced.
findings.matters: A sharp reduction in capital investment may indicate either prudent rebalancing or constrained capacity to invest in services and infrastructure, affecting the council's long-term service sustainability.
findings.figures: Total capital expenditure: £17.398m (2024/25) → £3.558m (2026/27); 'Our Place': £10.592m → £0.476m

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves declining 32% from £19.558m to £13.217m over three years
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves are being drawn down significantly from £19.558m (2024/25) to £13.217m (2026/27) and further declining to £11.737m (2028/29). This sustained reduction indicates substantial use of accumulated reserves.
findings.matters: Declining earmarked reserves indicate the council is either funding operations from accumulated resources or managing through a transition period with constrained capacity.

findings.headline: General Fund Balance reduced from £4.478m to £2.052m and held flat thereafter, only 9.6% of annual revenue expenditure
findings.detail: The General Fund Balance declined from £4.478m (2024/25) to £2.052m (2026/27) and is projected to remain flat through 2028/29. This represents only 9.6% of net revenue expenditure of £21.414m, suggesting the council has reached its minimum acceptable reserve level.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would be concerned that the council has reduced its financial buffer to the minimum, limiting its ability to absorb unexpected shocks or income shortfalls.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance: £4.478m (2024/25) → £2.052m (2026/27 onwards); Net Revenue Expenditure 2026/27: £21.414m

findings.headline: £30m commercial property investment programme with £0.733m valuation volatility reserve
findings.detail: The council has approved up to £30m for commercial property investment. To manage valuation risk, it has established a Valuation Volatility Earmarked Reserve of £0.733m (3% of portfolio purchase price). A Commercial Contingency revenue base budget is also included in the MTFP to mitigate yield risk. Assets are held for 5–10 years and are not liquid short-term.
findings.matters: A £30m capital commitment with explicit risk reserves signals material property valuation and income exposure. The need for a contingency budget indicates the council is concerned about achieving projected yields.
findings.figures: £30m investment approved; £0.733m valuation reserve (3% of purchase price); 5–10 year holding period
findings.quote: Up to £30m has been approved for investment in Commercial Property in support and protection of Council Services. A Valuation Volatility Earmarked Reserve has been created with a balance of £0.733m which reflects 3% of purchase price of the portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: Council tax at maximum referendum limit with no headroom for future increases
findings.detail: Council Tax is increasing by 2.97% in 2026/27, at the maximum allowable before triggering a referendum (3% or £5, whichever is greater). The MTFP assumes 2.99% increases in all future years. The council has no room to exceed this threshold and is reliant on the government maintaining the 3% threshold; any lower ceiling would immediately create a shortfall.
findings.matters: The council has used all available tax headroom. Future sustainability depends entirely on government continuing to allow maximum increases and on government grant changes.
findings.figures: 2026/27 increase: 2.97%; assumed ongoing: 2.99%; threshold: 3% or £5 (whichever greater)
findings.quote: The Budget for 2026/27 assumes that the Council approve a Council Tax of £256.14 (£248.76 2025/26), an increase of 2.97% being the maximum amount allowable under the Government's referendum limit of up to 3% or £5 (whichever is the greater).

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: Management restructure in progress; financial impact not yet quantified
findings.detail: A management restructure is undergoing formal consultation (14 Jan – 20 Feb 2026) with implementation by 1 April 2026. No cost estimate is provided in the budget. Restructure costs (redundancy, buyout, transition) could be material and may fall in 2026/27 or beyond.
findings.matters: A major organisational change with cost implications has been assumed in budget planning but the actual expense is unknown and deferred pending outcome of consultation.
findings.figures: Cost not quantified
findings.quote: A management restructure is currently subject to consultation, with the following timelines in place: Formal consultation commences Wednesday 14th January 2026 - minimum of 30 days

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: General Fund balance declining; reserve strategy depends heavily on earmarked drawdowns
findings.detail: The working General Fund balance falls from £2.198m to £2.052m (a reduction of £0.146m) by end of 2026/27 and stays flat at £2.052m thereafter. The council relies on £1.564m net contribution to earmarked reserves in 2026/27 and significant reserve use in 2027/28 (£0.349m) and 2028/29 (£0.681m) to balance the budget. Earmarked reserves themselves reduce from £14.042m to £13.250m by 2030/31.
findings.matters: The council has limited cushion; budget balance depends on drawing earmarked reserves, which narrows over time. Combined with unfunded gaps in years 4–5, resilience is constrained.
findings.figures: General Fund Working Balance: £2.052m (10–12% of budget requirement); Earmarked Reserves 2026/27: £13.212m; 2030/31: £13.250m; reserve drawdowns: £0.349m (27/28), £0.681m (28/29)
findings.quote: The movement on the General Fund Balance is a reduction of £0.146m and is forecast to be £2.052m at the end of 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility grant declining; assumed to reduce further over MTFP
findings.detail: The council receives a new Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant for waste collection costs. This grant is assumed to decline over the medium term as "producers change the packaging of their goods." The council has assumed £0.563m loss of EPR funding in 2026/27 alone, with further erosion expected.
findings.matters: A new but volatile income stream with structural decline built in; risk if actual decline is faster or if government policy changes.
findings.figures: £0.563m reduction in 2026/27; further decline assumed beyond
findings.quote: Extended Producer Responsibility funding - £0.563m reduction in Funding

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: Food Waste Collection service implementation adds £0.763m permanent expenditure in 2026/27
findings.detail: A new mandated service (food waste collection) launches in 2026/27, adding £0.763m to the base budget. While funded in year, this represents a new ongoing obligation without evidence the funding settles at sustainable levels.
findings.matters: A new statutory service with material cost in a year of tight funding; risk if waste collection grant changes or collections underperform.
findings.figures: £0.763m in 2026/27 and ongoing
findings.quote: £0.763m implementation of the Food Waste Collection service

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: £7.412m of the £12.164m capital programme (61%) is in early-stage pipeline; estimates could vary by 50%
findings.detail: Of the five-year capital programme totalling £12.164m, only £4.752m is approved for spending (Stage 3 and business-as-usual). The remaining £7.412m is pipeline projects at pre-stage and stage levels. The document explicitly states: "the estimates within this programme could go up and/or down by 50%." This creates significant forecast uncertainty.
findings.matters: Capital spending and its revenue consequences (borrowing cost, MRP) cannot be reliably forecast; actual spending and debt could deviate substantially.
findings.figures: £7.412m pipeline (61% of £12.164m total); variance range ±50%
findings.quote: There are a number of significant programmes of work, which at this time have not been the subject of a full financial appraisal, and to that end Members should be aware that the estimates within this programme could go up and/or down by 50%.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus ended entirely; £0.499m grant removed
findings.detail: The government terminated the New Homes Bonus scheme. The funding has been rolled into general revenue support grant, but the council is no longer receiving this £0.499m reward for housing growth. This removes a direct link between council housing delivery and income.
findings.matters: Removes financial incentive for new housing growth and reduces predictability of income tied to local activity.
findings.figures: £0.499m removed
findings.quote: The Council previously received New Homes Bonus from 2011/12 which was used to support economic growth initiatives in the district. The government has now stopped this funding and has rolled it into revenue support grant

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: Business rates income falls from £6.655m (2025/26) to £2.994m (2026/27) following government reset
findings.detail: Business rates income falls from £6.655m (2025/26) to £2.994m (2026/27)—a loss of £3.661m—because the government reset the business rates retention system and removed accumulated growth the council had built up above its baseline. This loss is partially offset by increased government grants (£4.313m), but represents a structural shift in the council's funding model with reduced control over growth.
findings.matters: Funding becomes more dependent on government grant allocation, reducing the council's own revenue-raising capacity and flexibility.
findings.quote: A reset of Business rates which removed previously accumulated growth and set a new funding baseline

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 27/28-31/32, the budget 27/28, capital programme 27/28 to 31/32
findings.headline: Unresolved funding gap of £1.66m appears in 2029/30 and 2030/31
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Analysis projects funding gaps of £773,500 in 2029/30 and £889,000 in 2030/31. The council acknowledges these are not yet funded and states that "efficiency savings will need to be found in the medium to longer term" dependent on local government reorganisation outcomes. Years 2026/27–2028/29 balance, but the plan breaks in years 4 and 5.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has a credible plan to bridge material gaps, and what drives dependency on external reorganisation decisions.
findings.quote: It is possible however that efficiency savings will need to be found in the medium to longer term, but this will be dependent on the future makeup of local government in Lincolnshire and future government funding levels.

findings.paper_title: Collection Fund - Council Tax Surplus 2025-26 & Council Tax Base 2026-27.
findings.headline: Collection Fund surplus is £62,800 lower than budgeted for 2025-26
findings.detail: The council's share of the Collection Fund surplus for 2025-26 is estimated at £212,800, representing a decrease of £62,800 from the £275,600 that was budgeted when setting the 2025/26 budget. This 22.8% variance means significantly less one-off income is available than was assumed in budget planning.
findings.matters: Collection Fund surpluses provide non-recurring income to support budgets; a material adverse variance suggests forecasting inaccuracy or external changes in the tax base, reducing cash available to smooth the 2026-27 budget.
findings.figures: £212,800 estimated vs £275,600 budgeted; variance of £62,800 (22.8% shortfall)
findings.quote: The surplus share of £ 212,800 represents a decrease of £62,800 against the 2025/26 budgeted surplus of £275,600.

findings.headline: Business rates revaluation reset on 1 April 2026 will require at least £1.3m from volatility reserves to manage income impact
findings.detail: The government announced a business rates revaluation reset effective 1 April 2026 that will reset rateable values. External advice indicates the council will need at least £1.3m from its Business Rates Volatility Reserve to cushion the impact. The reserve currently holds £2.677m after adjustment for anticipated impact.
findings.matters: This is a concrete identified funding shortfall in 2026/27 that will require material reserve drawdown. The council is already provisioning for a material adverse impact to business rates income.
findings.figures: £1.3m needed; Business Rates Volatility Reserve balance £2.677m (adjusted)
findings.quote: External advice has suggested that at least £1.3m of this reserve will be needed to fund the business rates reset in 2026/2027.

findings.headline: £8m of reserves allocated for reprioritisation without yet specifying where it will be spent
findings.detail: The Corporate Policy and Resources Committee approved allocation of £8m from usable reserves to fund future corporate priorities in June 2025. However, the specific projects and allocation have not been determined; this will come when the Corporate Plan is finalised.
findings.matters: Uncommitted drawdown at this scale creates governance risk; the council has reserved large funds for unspecified purposes without business cases or clear priorities.
findings.quote: The Corporate Plan is under development and once finalised a separate report will be brought to members to discuss the specific allocation of the £8m to align to corporate priorities.

findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to fall 37% over six years from £28.586m to £18.027m
findings.detail: Total usable reserves of £28.586m as of 31 March 2025 are forecast to reduce to £18.027m by 31 March 2031. The decline includes £12.586m to fund capital expenditure and £5.598m to fund revenue from reserves, partially offset by £15.625m in new contributions.
findings.matters: A large reduction in reserves reduces the council's financial flexibility for unexpected pressures and indicates material drawdown of accumulated buffers over the planning period.
findings.quote: After taking account of all approved movements the forecast balance as of 31st March 2031 is £18.027m, a reduction of £10.559m.

findings.headline: Multiple unresolved IT control deficiencies in core finance system (One Finance)
findings.detail: Four general IT control deficiencies were identified: password settings below policy standards, user access granted without documented approval, three finance team members assigned inappropriate privileged access, and system changes implemented without formal approval. While auditors assessed material misstatement risk as remote, they note these deficiencies 'collectively weaken the overall control environment'.
findings.matters: Weak IT access controls and change management procedures increase risk of unauthorised data access, system manipulation, and potential fraudulent transactions affecting financial records
findings.figures: Four deficiencies identified; three finance staff with inappropriate privileged access
findings.quote: these deficiencies increase the risk of unauthorised access, inappropriate changes, and potential misuse of privileged rights, which could compromise system integrity and sensitive financial data.

findings.headline: Material related party transactions were omitted from draft financial statements
findings.detail: The audit identified material related party transactions that were missing from the draft accounts and had to be corrected. This represents a control failure in the council's related party identification and disclosure process.
findings.matters: Undisclosed related party transactions obscure actual financial relationships and suggest governance weaknesses or inadequate oversight of conflicts of interest
findings.figures: Not quantified in available text
findings.quote: Material related party transactions were omitted from the draft accounts, which could compromise the quality and transparency of the financial statements by failing to fully disclose the Council's financial relationships.

findings.headline: Significant control weaknesses over high-value property valuations not meeting audit standards
findings.detail: The council lacks satisfactory management review controls for valuation of £35m in land and buildings and £22.9m in investment property, despite these being significant audit risks. The council instead relies solely on external valuers' professionalism without independent internal controls meeting auditing standards.
findings.matters: Weak controls over major asset values (totalling c.£58m) create risk of valuation errors going undetected; reliance on external experts without independent review is below best practice
findings.figures: £35m in land and buildings; £22.9m in investment properties
findings.quote: Auditing Standards requires auditors to identify a management review control (MRC) where there is a significant audit risk... We note that although the Council has processes in place... these processes do not meet the required threshold of an MRC.

findings.headline: Uncorrected audit misstatement of £0.3m arising from incorrect property classification
findings.detail: Three sites/properties valued at approximately £0.8m were incorrectly classified as 'non-specialised land and buildings' under Existing Use Value methodology when they should have been classified as investment properties under Fair Value methodology. The council did not correct this misstatement despite audit identification.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements undermine the reliability of financial statements and signal either weak financial controls or unwillingness to correct identified errors
findings.figures: £0.3m impact on reported deficit (3.8%); £0.8m in misclassified assets
findings.quote: we have identified one misstatement concerning the classification of three sites/properties having total value of c.£0.8m. These assets were recorded as non-specialised land and buildings and valued at year-end using the Existing Use Value (EUV) methodology. In fact, they should have been classified as investment properties

findings.headline: No formal savings programme despite previously identified funding gaps from 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: The council was advised in the prior year that 'The General Fund reserve will be insufficient to bridge funding gaps' from 2026/27 onwards, yet has not implemented a formal savings programme. The council is delaying action pending government decisions on funding methodology and business rates changes, creating a reactive rather than proactive posture.
findings.matters: Known funding shortfalls with no advance mitigation plan indicates poor financial resilience and increases risk of forced spending cuts or reserve depletion
findings.figures: Funding gaps identified from 2026/27 onwards; no savings programme currently in place
findings.quote: The Council does not currently have a savings programme. Whilst the Council's medium term financial plan, which was approved in March 2025, does have funding gaps for 2026/27 onwards, it is not clear at this point whether these will be realised.

findings.headline: Council will cease to exist as a standalone entity, being merged into a new unitary authority by 1 April 2028
findings.detail: West Lindsey will be incorporated into a newly created authority as part of local government reorganisation affecting two-tier areas. This merger is described as 'still at an early stage' but will have 'a large number of impacts on the Council's operating model', including uncertainty about whether funds will be needed to implement the new authority structure.
findings.matters: The certain cessation of the council within three years creates fundamental uncertainty about entity continuity, borrowing repayment obligations, service delivery, and the basis for any multi-year lending decisions
findings.figures: Merger deadline: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: West Lindsey District Council in its current form will not exist after 1st April 2028 as it will be within a newly created authority.

findings.headline: 2024/25 budget balanced largely by one-off business rates surplus; 2025/26 similarly dependent on one-time benefit
findings.detail: While West Lindsey delivered a £1.8m underspend in 2024/25 (outturn £16.2m against revised budget of £18m), the 2025/26 budget of £21.15m is described as 'balanced largely due to a one-off business rates surplus'. This indicates underlying structural pressures are masked by non-recurring items. Officers are now focused on addressing future budget gaps within the MTFP.
findings.matters: A budget balanced through one-off items rather than sustainable service delivery is fragile. It masks the need for permanent cost control and suggests underlying spending pressures are not being addressed structurally.
findings.figures: 2024/25: underspend of £1.8m on revised budget of £18m. 2025/26 budget: £21.15m, balanced by one-off business rates surplus.
findings.quote: The Council's Net Revenue Expenditure budget for 2025/26 has been set at approximately £21.15m... While the 2025/26 budget is balanced largely due to a one-off business rates surplus, officers are now focused on addressing future budget gaps within the Medium Term Financial Plan.

findings.headline: Governance policies overdue for review; anti-fraud policy not updated since 2019
findings.detail: The audit notes that several governance policies, including the Officer Code of Conduct and disciplinary policies, are overdue for review despite a mandated two-year review cycle. The Prevention of Financial Crime and Anti-Fraud and Corruption Policy was last updated in March 2019 and is significantly out of date. A Performance Improvement Observation has been raised on both governance and anti-fraud policy currency.
findings.matters: Outdated governance and anti-fraud policies create control gaps and suggest that governance processes have not been maintained with appropriate rigour. This can indicate broader governance discipline issues.
findings.figures: Anti-fraud policy last updated: March 2019 (6+ years old at audit date). Officer Code of Conduct and disciplinary policies: overdue for review per mandated two-year cycle.
findings.quote: The 'Officer Code of Conduct' sets standards for staff behaviour, covering anti-fraud, anti-corruption, gifts and hospitality, and requiring disclosure of relationships with contractors... However, several related policies, including the Code of Conduct (last reviewed in 2020) and disciplinary policies, are overdue for review despite a two-year cycle.

findings.headline: Recent turnover of S151 Officer and Chief Executive during 2024/25 indicates governance instability
findings.detail: West Lindsey appointed a permanent Section 151 Officer in May 2025 following an interim arrangement from February to May. It also appointed a new Chief Executive in July 2025 who formally commenced in September, with interim cover during the transition. In September, a new Leader and Deputy Leader were appointed following the removal of former office holders. While the audit states these appointments 'ensured continuity and strengthened governance', the turnover itself indicates recent instability.
findings.matters: Continuous churn of chief finance and chief executive officers can disrupt strategic planning and financial control. Lenders monitor leadership stability as an indicator of governance quality and strategic continuity.
findings.figures: S151 Officer interim gap: February-May 2025. Chief Executive interim gap: July-September 2025. Leader/Deputy Leader replaced September 2025.
findings.quote: In May 2025, the Council confirmed the appointment of a permanent Section 151 Officer, following an interim arrangement in place from February to May 2025. Also, in July 2025, the Council appointed a new Chief Executive, who formally commenced duties in September 2025.

findings.headline: Council has no formalised savings plan despite facing funding gaps from 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: The audit identifies that West Lindsey lacks a structured process for identifying and delivering savings, relying instead on its historically adequate reserves. However, the Medium Term Financial Plan projects funding gaps of £1.2m in 2026/27, growing to £2.9m by 2027/28 and £3.5m thereafter. The council currently plans to bridge these with reserves, but lacks formal arrangements to ensure savings are delivered when required.
findings.matters: A council facing predictable funding gaps without formalized efficiency arrangements poses credit risk. Lenders need confidence that councils can deliver savings when required; relying on reserve drawdown alone is unsustainable.
findings.figures: Funding gaps: £nil (2025/26), £1.2m (2026/27), £2.9m (2027/28), £3.5m (2028/29), £3.5m (2029/30). Current usable reserves: £28.6m, projected to remain £20-21m through MTFP period.
findings.quote: the absence of structured savings arrangements presents a potential future risk—particularly from 2026/27 onwards, when General Fund reserves are projected to be insufficient to cover anticipated funding gaps
